memory_update.text: Technology theme should be decomposed from AI/cloud/software headlines into physical and control-plane bottlenecks: semicap subsystems, packaging/test, optical materials, epitaxy tools, data-center power/thermal, and cloud security automation.
Semiconductor equipment subsystem suppliers are a priority underfollowed lane because they may be embedded across many fab tools while remaining less visible than tool OEMs or fabs.

Advanced packaging and backend test overflow are likely key AI semiconductor bottleneck nodes, especially where HBM and advanced logic consume internal capacity and push lower-margin or conventional work outward.
Optical interconnect materials and compound semiconductor epitaxy tools are promising second-order discovery lanes tied to AI networking bandwidth growth.
Data-center electrical and thermal balance-of-plant should be searched beyond obvious leaders, focusing on component suppliers, qualification-heavy vendors, and field-service bottlenecks.
Before moving to Layer 1B, verify current public candidates using filings, market caps, analyst coverage, segment revenue, backlog, customer evidence, and capex linkage.

layer1a.summary: Broad technology decomposes into several physical and software bottleneck lanes: AI compute demand, cloud data-center buildout, semiconductor manufacturing complexity, optical interconnect scaling, power/grid constraints, cybersecurity and automation spend. For Layer 1A, the highest-quality decomposition should avoid starting with mega-cap AI leaders and instead map the second-order nodes that enable them: semiconductor tool subsystems, advanced packaging and test overflow, optical/compound-semiconductor materials and epitaxy tools, data-center electrical/thermal infrastructure, cloud/cybersecurity automation layers, and grid/power execution assets. The strongest underfollowed discovery setup is where demand is visible at the hyperscaler or semiconductor leader level, but the constrained supplier sits one or two steps upstream with low analyst mindshare, strict qualification, long lead times, or recurring consumables.

supply_chain_nodes.bottleneck_hypothesis: The market may over-focus on visible tool OEMs while underpricing the niche suppliers embedded across many tools. These suppliers can gain broad exposure to fab capex without needing to win a single end-customer chip design.
supply_chain_nodes.market_cap_hunting_notes: Prioritize USD 1B-15B industrial technology and semiconductor-equipment suppliers; include USD 300M-1B only if filings show real semi exposure and customer concentration is manageable.
supply_chain_nodes.node: Semiconductor equipment subsystems: vacuum, RF power, gas flow, measurement, motion control, and process-control components embedded inside larger wafer-fab tools
supply_chain_nodes.public_asset_hunting_notes: Start from reference leaders ASML, Applied Materials, Lam Research, Tokyo Electron, and KLA, then map their suppliers and public subsystem vendors. Search for companies with recurring consumables, high installed-base exposure, proprietary process know-how, and evidence that their parts are qualified across many tool platforms.

theme_map.public_market_search_strategy: Use a two-lane funnel. Lane 1 maps reference leaders such as NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom, TSMC, ASML, hyperscalers, Arista, Vertiv, Eaton, and major cybersecurity/cloud software firms only to identify where capex and system requirements are moving. Lane 2 searches for less obvious public suppliers with narrow but necessary roles: tool subsystems, process control, vacuum and gas equipment, specialty chemicals, plating chemistry, OSAT/backend test, optical substrates, epitaxy tools, contract manufacturing, data-center electrical components, transformer fluids, cooling parts, secure automation software, identity infrastructure, and compliance-heavy distributors. Prefer public companies with USD 300M-10B market caps when possible, USD 10B-30B only for unusually pure exposure, and micro-caps only as speculative shadow leads.
supply_side_constraints: Long qualification cycles for semiconductor equipment subsystems and materials
Concentrated supplier base in niche semiconductor process components such as vacuum, RF power, gas flow, metrology, and motion control
Advanced packaging and backend test capacity competing for HBM, logic, DDR, and NAND workloads
Potential concentration in optical materials such as indium phosphide substrates and qualified epitaxy capacity
Electrical equipment, transformers, switchgear, thermal systems, and grid construction constrained by manufacturing capacity and utility procurement cycles
Software monetization risk where AI features are adopted faster than customers are willing to pay incremental software margins
